name: Hough Reclamation
description:
Hough burned in 1966. That is the fact that every history of this neighborhood begins with, and the fact that the neighborhood has spent a century and a half trying to transcend. The riots — sparked by racial segregation, police brutality, and the concentrated poverty that American cities engineered with surgical precision — destroyed four square blocks and killed four people. The rebuilding never really happened. Decades of disinvestment followed, the same pattern repeated across Black neighborhoods in every American city: capital withdrawn, services reduced, population blamed for the conditions capital created.

By 2140, when the corridor was taking shape and corponations were claiming sovereign territory across the Great Lakes region, Hough was among the neighborhoods that nobody claimed. Too poor, too depopulated, too much liability. What happened next was not planned by any corponation or government. The remaining residents — predominantly Black families who had held their homes through every wave of abandonment — began the Reclamation. Using salvaged materials, cooperative labor, and technology acquired through the excluded economy, they rebuilt the neighborhood on their own terms. Vertical farms in converted apartment buildings. Solar arrays on every rooftop. A mesh communication network that operates independently of Saltmarsh's signal grid. A community governance model based on block councils that traces its organizational DNA back to the mutual aid societies that sustained Black communities through Jim Crow.

Hough Reclamation is now the most self-sufficient neighborhood in the Cleveland sprawl. It generates 80% of its own power, grows 60% of its own food, and maintains its own communications infrastructure. It is also, by every corporate metric, one of the poorest — because the metrics don't measure what Hough has built. The corponations have taken notice. Tollgate has offered infrastructure integration three times. Tessera has proposed a 'community cognitive wellness partnership.' Each offer has been declined by the block councils with the same response: 'We remember what your help looks like.' The phrase has become a neighborhood motto, painted on walls and printed on the mesh network's welcome screen.

sights: Vertical farms visible through apartment windows — green light from grow systems casting the streets in an agricultural glow at night
Solar arrays on every rooftop, some salvaged, some fabricated locally, none matching — a patchwork of self-sufficiency
Murals commemorating 1966, painted and repainted by each generation, the imagery evolving but the memory constant
Block council meeting halls — converted storefronts with reinforced doors and mesh network nodes mounted on the roof
The Welcome Wall at the neighborhood's eastern boundary: 'We Remember What Your Help Looks Like'
sounds: The hum of vertical farm systems — pumps, fans, grow lights cycling in a rhythm that has replaced the old industrial noise
Mesh network chatter — Hough's independent communication system carries voice, text, and community broadcasts on frequencies Saltmarsh doesn't control
Block council meetings — democracy conducted in person, in rooms, with voices raised and votes counted by hand
Music — Hough's sound system, run through the mesh network, plays a community-curated stream that mixes everything from gospel to electronic
The absence of corporate sound — no advertisements, no drone traffic, no algorithmic ambient programming
smells: Growing things — the vegetable-rich scent of the vertical farms permeates every block within a two-street radius
Cooking — community kitchens operate on block rotation, feeding residents who contribute labor hours to the Reclamation's shared infrastructure
Clean air — Hough's rooftop gardens and biofilter systems produce noticeably better air quality than surrounding neighborhoods
atmosphere.feel: Hough Reclamation feels like a dare. It dares the corridor to function without it. It dares the corponations to explain why a neighborhood with no corporate investment has better air, better food, and better community health than the zones that spent trillions on infrastructure. It is not utopia — the block councils argue, resources are scarce, and the independence that defines the neighborhood also isolates it. But it is real in a way that most of the corridor has forgotten how to be.

demographics: Approximately 14,000 residents, predominantly Black families with multi-generational roots in the neighborhood. Significant population of climate refugees who were accepted by the block councils through a formal community sponsorship process. Almost entirely Tier 1 and excluded by corporate classification, though the residents reject the tier system entirely. Augmentation rates are low — approximately 15% — by choice as much as economics.
economy: Cooperative and non-monetary. The Reclamation operates on a labor-credit system where residents contribute hours to shared infrastructure — farming, maintenance, teaching, security — and receive credits redeemable for goods and services within the neighborhood. External trade is conducted through designated brokers who interface with the excluded economy. The block councils collectively hold a modest Q reserve for essential purchases that cannot be produced internally.
power_structure: Direct democracy through block councils. Each residential block elects a council of five. The councils send representatives to the Hough Assembly, which meets monthly to address neighborhood-wide issues. Decisions require two-thirds majority. There is no executive authority. The system is slow, contentious, and functional — the opposite of corporate governance in every respect.
dangers: Resource scarcity — self-sufficiency is 80%, not 100%, and the remaining 20% creates vulnerability to external supply disruptions
Corporate encroachment — Tollgate's infrastructure integration offers become less optional with each refusal
Internal tension — the block council system produces legitimate disagreements about resource allocation that sometimes escalate
Medical limitations — Hough's community health practitioners are skilled but lack access to advanced diagnostics and surgical capability
Isolation — independence from the corridor's systems also means independence from its protections, such as they are
opportunities: The Reclamation model is being studied and replicated by excluded communities across the corridor — Hough is becoming a template
The mesh network is the only independent communications infrastructure in the Cleveland sprawl, making it invaluable to anyone who needs to communicate off Saltmarsh's grid
Hough's vertical farming expertise is a tradeable skill set — other neighborhoods pay in materials and favors for agricultural consulting
The block councils' rejection of corporate offers has earned them respect and political capital among the corridor's excluded population
story_hooks: Tessera has changed tactics — instead of offering partnership, they've begun offering free NovaMind Basic implants to Hough's teenagers, and some are accepting
The mesh network has intercepted transmissions that appear to originate from inside Tollgate's infrastructure — someone inside the corponation is trying to communicate with the Reclamation
A block council vote on whether to accept Tollgate's latest infrastructure offer has split the Assembly down the middle, threatening the neighborhood's governance model
frequented_by: Hough residents — the Reclamation is home, not a destination
Excluded community organizers studying the Reclamation model
Operators who need access to the mesh network for off-grid communication
Tessera recruiters, increasingly unwelcome, working the neighborhood's edges

notable_locations.name: Block Zero
notable_locations.description: The four blocks that burned in 1966 — now the site of the Reclamation's largest vertical farm and the Hough Assembly meeting hall

notable_locations.name: The Welcome Wall
notable_locations.description: The eastern boundary marker bearing the neighborhood motto — part public art, part political statement, part warning

notable_locations.name: The Mesh Tower
notable_locations.description: A repurposed water tower housing the primary node of Hough's independent communications network — the neighborhood's most strategically valuable asset
